title: Valid Mountain Array
prompt: Given an array of integers `arr`, return `true` if and only if it is a valid mountain array. An array is a mountain array if `arr.length >= 3` and there exists some index `i` with `0 < i < arr.length - 1` such that `arr[0] < arr[1] < ... < arr[i]` (strictly increasing up to the peak) and `arr[i] > arr[i+1] > ... > arr[arr.length - 1]` (strictly decreasing after it). The peak cannot be the first or last element.

examples.explanation: Not strictly increasing before the peak (5 == 5).

hints: You could scan to find the maximum and separately verify both sides increase/decrease strictly, but that's two passes — can you do it with two pointers walking inward from each end?
Walk a pointer up from the left while values strictly increase, and a pointer up from the right while values strictly increase going backward.
It's a valid mountain exactly when both pointers meet at the same index, and that index is neither the first nor the last position.

solution.approach: Use two pointers starting at each end. Advance the left pointer while the array is strictly increasing, and advance the right pointer leftward while the array is strictly increasing walking backward from the end. If arr is a true mountain, both pointers climb toward the same peak and meet there; the array is valid only if they land on the same index, and that index isn't the very first or very last element (which would mean the whole array is monotonic instead of a mountain).
